segments.translit: jñānāmṛtaparituṣṭo hi kṛṣṇācāryyapādas tam evārthaṃ pratipādayati —
segments.translation: The master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, contented with the [nectar]{amrta} of [knowledge]{jnana}, sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta opens with his stock formula: the master Kāṇha, contented with the nectar of knowledge, sets forth 'that same meaning', without saying which. The Tibetan translation agrees word for word (ye shes kyi bdud rtsis yongs su tshim pa) (cp.42.m1).

flags.note: 'That same meaning' (tam evārtham) is Munidatta's stock opening for a song (cp.42.m1), not necessarily a pointer back to song 41. The Tibetan has de nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of that very thing'.

segments.translit:
cia ityādi | sahajenetyādi | prakṛtisvarūpeṇa sarvvadaiva ṣoḍaśīśūnyatāyā[ṃ] saṃpūrṇo 'yaṃ mama cittarājaḥ | ata eva skandhaviyogeneti | bho janā mama skandhābhāvāt viṣāda[ṃ] mā kuru ||
tathā ca hevajre —
skandhābhāvaparamam iti |
segments.translation: 'The [mind]{citta}…' and so on. '[Innately]{sahaja}…' and so on: that is, by its natural [true nature]{svarupa}, this [king of mind]{king-of-mind} of mine is always filled with the [sixteen emptinesses]{sixteen-emptinesses}. Therefore, 'at separation from the [aggregates]{skandha}': O people, do not be [dejected]{visanna} at the absence of my [aggregates]{skandha}. And so it is said in the [Hevajra]{tx-hevajra}: 'The absence of the [aggregates]{skandha} is supreme.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads sahaje as sahajena, 'innately', glossed 'by its natural true nature' (the draft has 'in the innate'): the king of his mind is always filled with the sixteen emptinesses, so no one should grieve that his aggregates are gone; he cites the Hevajra. The Tibetan has 'all the gods' for sarvadaiva, 'always' (cp.42.m2).

equations.en: by its natural true nature (prakṛtisvarūpeṇa): innately, by nature

flags.note: Munidatta cites the song's sahaje as sahajena and glosses it prakṛtisvarūpeṇa, 'by its natural true nature' (cp.42.m2): an adverbial 'innately, by nature', where the draft of 1a takes a locative, 'in the innate'. The Tibetan cites only lhan cig skyes pa, 'innate', with no case ending, so it does not decide the point.

Where Munidatta has sarvadaiva, 'always' (cp.42.m2), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lha thams cad, 'all the gods', as if reading sarvadeva. It also has 'di dag gi, 'of these', for mama, 'my', so that in the Tibetan the sixteen emptinesses fill 'all the gods of natural own-being' and the king of mind is theirs. Its comment has sdug bsngal, 'suffering', for viṣāda, and bral ba, 'separated', for abhāva.

Shastri restores ṣoḍaśīśūnyatāyā[ṃ], a locative ('complete in'). Unrestored, the form could stand for an instrumental, śūnyatayā, 'filled with', which the Tibetan gis supports and the song's śūṇa saṃpunnā suits; I translate 'filled with'. Ṣoḍaśī could also mean 'sixteenth'; the Tibetan stong pa nyid bcu drug has 'sixteen'.

The Hevajra quotation, skandhābhāvaparamam iti, looks truncated. The Tibetan has a whole line, phung po dngos med bde ba'i mchog, 'the absence of the aggregates is supreme bliss', with a 'bliss' the Sanskrit lacks. I translate only the Sanskrit, and have not located the line in the Hevajra.
bho janā, 'O people', is plural, but the prohibition mā kuru is singular; the Tibetan has the plural skye bo rnams with ma byed cig.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena svarūpaṃ pratipādayati —
bho bālayogin vada kathaṃ kṛṣṇācāryyo hi [60ka] na vidyate trailokyasvarūpaṃ ta[ṃ] [vi]bhāvya | anudinaṃ sphurati paramārthajaladhau krīḍatīty arthaḥ |
tathā cāgama[ḥ] —
yathā nadījalāt svacchāt mīna(ne) utpatati drutam |
sarvvaśūnyāt tathā svacchāt māyājālam udīryyate ||
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he sets forth the [true nature]{svarupa}: 'O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, say, how could the master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} not exist?' Having discerned that [true nature]{svarupa} of the [three worlds]{trailokya}, 'he [radiates]{sphurana} day after day': the meaning is, he [plays]{lila} in the [ocean]{ocean} of the [ultimate]{paramartha}. And so [scripture]{agama} says: 'As a fish leaps swiftly up from the clear water of a [river]{river}, so from the clear [all-empty]{sarvasunya} the [net of illusion]{mayajala} is sent forth.'
segments.note: Munidatta reads pharai as sphurati: Kāṇha radiates day after day, that is, plays in the ocean of the ultimate. His gerund vibhāvya, 'having discerned' the three worlds' true nature, stands where the song has pamāi, so he seems to take pamāi as a gerund too ('having measured, come to know'?), not the draft's finite 'spans' (cp.42.m3).

equations.en: he plays in the ocean of the ultimate (paramārthajaladhau krīḍati)

citations.quoted: yathā nadījalāt svacchāt mīna utpatati drutam | sarvaśūnyāt tathā svacchāt māyājālam udīryate
citations.work: unnamed 'scripture' (āgama); perhaps the Pañcakrama, whose completion-stage teaching has illusion arise from the all-empty

flags.note: pamāi (2b): Munidatta's vibhāvya (cp.42.m3) is an absolutive, and Old Bengali absolutives end in -i (dekhi, 'having seen', in 3a), which suggests he took pamāi as one too, perhaps from pra-mā, 'measure, come to know': 'he radiates day after day, having taken the measure of the three worlds'. The draft's 'and spans' makes it a second finite verb.

ta[ṃ] [vi]bhāvya rests on two restorations by Shastri. The Tibetan comment, 'jig rten gyi ngo bo de'i bsgom par bya'o, 'that nature of the world is to be meditated on', reads bhāvya as a gerundive without vi-, and has 'world' ('jig rten) for trailokya. I follow Shastri's vibhāvya.

Shastri's daṇḍa falls after vibhāvya, which would attach the gerund to the question ('how could Kāṇha, having discerned that true nature, not exist?'). I attach it to 'he radiates', which follows the order of 2b; the Tibetan ends a sentence after bsgom par bya'o.

The Tibetan line of 2b is in the first person: bdag ni khams gsum gtan du 'phro, 'I constantly radiate through the three realms', with nothing for pamāi. Munidatta's comment and its Tibetan keep the third person (cp.42.m3).

The fish is missing from the Tibetan of the quoted verse: for mīna utpatati drutam, 'a fish leaps swiftly up' (the verse's second quarter), it has bdag gi ngo bo myur du bskyed, 'one's own nature is swiftly produced'; for udīryate, 'is sent forth', it has ston par byed, 'displays'. Shastri prints mīna(ne), apparently recording a manuscript mīne; the fish itself is clear in the Sanskrit.

sarvaśūnya, 'the all-empty', is the Guhyasamāja name for the fourth emptiness, clear light, not plain emptiness (śūnyatā), so I propose an entry (sarvasunya) rather than tag it sunyata. The Tibetan has stong nyid kun dangs, 'emptiness, all clear'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena dṛṣṭāntadvāreṇa tam evārthaṃ vispaṣṭayati —
mūṛhā ityādi | nīlapītādivarṇasaṃsthāno hi yo bhāvas tasya bhaṃgaṃ dṛṣṭvā mūrkhāḥ kimarthaṃ kātarā bhavanti(ti) | kim ambhodher bhagnataraṅgaṃ taṃ sāgaraṃ śoṣayatīti |
segments.translation: With the second [verse]{pada} he makes that same meaning plain by way of an example: '[Fools]{mudha}…' and so on. Why do [fools]{mudha}, seeing the destruction of a thing that has [colour]{varna} and shape, such as blue or yellow, become dismayed? Does the sea's broken [wave]{wave} dry up that [ocean]{ocean}?
segments.note: Munidatta takes couplet 3, his second verse, as an example: fools are dismayed to see a thing with colour and shape, blue or yellow, destroyed; but does a broken wave dry up the ocean? The wave answers to the destroyed thing; what the ocean is he does not say. The Tibetan line has 'the ocean parted from its waves' (cp.42.m4).

flags.note: The Tibetan line of 3b reads rlabs bral rgya mtsho, 'the ocean parted from its waves', taking bhāga as separation. Munidatta's bhagnataraṅgam, 'the broken wave', and the Tibetan comment's rlabs zhig pa, 'the waves broken', read it as bhagna (cp.42.m4).

The destruction of the thing is not glossed as the wave: Munidatta paraphrases 3a (what is seen, a thing with colour and shape; destroyed) and offers 3b as its example (dṛṣṭānta), so I give no equation (cp.42.m4).
Where the Sanskrit has kātarā bhavanti, 'become dismayed', the Tibetan comment has 'jig par byed, 'destroy', probably a slip for 'jigs, 'fear'.
Shastri prints bhavanti(ti): the plural agrees with mūrkhāḥ, and the manuscript apparently has the singular bhavati.

bhāva here is 'a thing', an entity with colour and shape, not the abstract 'being' of the bhava-being entry, so I leave it untagged. Ambhodhi and sāgara both mean 'ocean'; I use 'sea' for the first and tag the second.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena pariniṣpannatām āha —
bhava jāiṇa ityādi || sadgurupaṅkaja(jā)rajaḥ na karotīty arthaḥ | etadbhavasvabhāvaparijñānena kṛṣṇācāryyapādo bhave 'py atra vilasati krīḍatīti || 42 ||
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [perfected state]{parinispanna}: 'In this [existence]{bhava} no one goes…' and so on. The meaning is: owing to the dust of the true [guru]{guru}'s [lotus]{lotus} feet, he does not do so. Through fully knowing the [nature]{svabhava} of this [existence]{bhava}, the master [Kāṇha]{p-kanha} [plays]{lila} even here in [existence]{bhava}, that is, he sports.
segments.note: Munidatta calls couplet 5 his third verse, on the perfected state (the Tibetan: fourth), a count skipping couplet 4 that fits the loss of his comment there. By the true guru's grace there is no going or coming; knowing the nature of 'this existence' (etadbhava: 5a's esu read as 'this', as in the draft), Kāṇha plays even in existence (cp.42.m5).

flags.note: sadgurupaṅkaja(jā)rajaḥ na karotīty arthaḥ is hard to construe: as printed, 'the dust of the true guru's lotus does not do (it)'. I read rajaḥ as if instrumental, 'by the dust', with the Tibetan bla ma dam pa'i chu skyes kyi rdul gyis byed pa'i phyir ro, 'because it is done by the dust of the true guru's lotus', which, however, has no negative. 'He does not do so' takes na karoti as answering the song's ṇa (jāi, ābai) (cp.42.m5).

The Tibetan calls couplet 5 its fourth verse (rkang pa bzhi pas) and couplet 4 its third (cp.42.m6); Munidatta's tṛtīyapadena counts couplet 5 as the third, as if no comment on couplet 4 came before it (cp.42.m5).

etadbhava (cp.42.m5): 'this existence' takes 5a's esu as 'this' (Sanskrit etad) with bhaba, as the draft's 'this existence' does, and reads the line as stating the nature of existence: no going, no coming. His atra, 'here', may echo esu as well. The Tibetan line also has srid pa 'di, 'this existence', but makes the line a question with gang, 'what?'; the Tibetan comment has 'dir, 'here'.
paṅkaja is only 'lotus'; 'lotus feet' spells out the usual image (compare gurucaraṇareṇu, 'the dust of the guru's feet'). Rajas means both 'dust' and 'pollen'.

segments.translit: /rkang pa gsum pas de nyid brtan par byed do/ /rmongs pa zhes pa ni de bzhin du blun pos yod bzhin pa yang 'o ma'i nang na mar mi mthong ba'o/ /de bzhin du 'jig rten gsum mthong bzhin pa yang mi mthong ba'o/
segments.translation: With the third [verse]{pada} he makes that same point firm. '[Foolish]{mudha}': in the same way, a [fool]{mudha} does not see the [butter]{butter} in the [milk]{milk}, even though it is there. In the same way, even while seeing the [three worlds]{trailokya}, he does not see them.
segments.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) supplies this comment on couplet 4: it is the Tibetan translators' text, not Munidatta's Sanskrit, which is lost (cp.42.m6). It explains rmongs pa, 'foolish', as blun po, a fool who does not see the butter (mar) in milk though it is there, and likewise sees the three worlds without seeing them.

flags.note: Munidatta's Sanskrit comment on couplet 4 is lost: the Nepal manuscript passes from couplet 3 to couplet 5. This segment translates the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) and should be presented as the Tibetan translators' comment, not as Munidatta's words (cp.42.m6).

The last sentence, 'jig rten gsum mthong bzhin pa yang mi mthong ba'o, leaves unstated who does not see and what is missed: 'though seeing the three worlds, he does not see them'. The comment confirms mar, 'butter', for the obscure laṛa of 4b.

proposals.definition: The all-empty (sarvaśūnya): in the Guhyasamāja completion stage, the fourth and subtlest of four emptinesses, after the empty, the very empty and the greatly empty; another name for clear light. In the scripture verse Munidatta quotes on song 42, the net of illusion is sent forth from the clear all-empty as a fish leaps from clear water (cp.42.m3).
proposals.rationale: Munidatta's verse (cp.42.m3) uses sarvaśūnya as a technical term, not plain emptiness (śūnyatā); the glossary's three-emptinesses entry already names 'the all-empty' after them. The Tibetan reads stong nyid kun dangs, 'emptiness, all clear', apparently taking sarva with svaccha, so the Tibetan form is a loose match. Not the 'all is empty' of sarvaśūnyapramāṇa (cp.39.m4).

questions: 1a: Munidatta cites sahaje as sahajena, 'innately, by nature', glossed prakṛtisvarūpeṇa (cp.42.m2). The draft's 'in the innate' follows the locative. Keep the line and leave his reading to the note, or revisit it?

2b: Munidatta's absolutive vibhāvya stands where the song has pamāi (cp.42.m3), which suggests 'He radiates day after day, having taken the measure of the three worlds' rather than 'and spans the three worlds'. Would you revisit the draft line?
Names: I render Munidatta's Kṛṣṇācāryapāda as 'the master Kāṇha' to follow p-kanha (cp.42.m1, cp.42.m3, cp.42.m5). Would you rather keep his Sanskrit form, Kṛṣṇācārya, in the commentary?

cp.42.m5: I read sadgurupaṅkajarajaḥ na karoti with the Tibetan as 'owing to the dust of the true guru's lotus feet, he does not do so', treating rajaḥ as if instrumental (rajasā). Acceptable, or should the translation keep the printed nominative and simply be flagged as obscure?

Munidatta's 'third verse' for couplet 5 (cp.42.m5) suggests his comment on couplet 4 was already missing when the Nepal line was numbered, not lost later by damage. Is that worth saying in the edition, or too speculative?

cp.42.m6 is labelled as the Tibetan translators' comment, as asked. Glossary entries for song 23 attribute Tibetan-only comments to Munidatta ('per Munidatta, cp.23.m2'). Should the edition use one convention for both cases?
Should sarvasunya ('the all-empty') become an entry, or would you rather tag sarvaśūnya in cp.42.m3 as emptiness (sunyata)?
The scripture verse in cp.42.m3 (a fish leaping from clear water) reads like Guhyasamāja completion-stage literature, perhaps the Pañcakrama; I could not check it. Confirm, or drop the guess?
